full_text_en:
Bank of China Xinjiang Branch v. Xinxing Company — Letter of Credit Dispute

Plaintiff: Bank of China Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region Branch.

Legal Representative: Kang Mei, Branch Manager.

Agent ad litem: Zhang Yumei, Chief of the International Settlement Division, Bank of China Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region Branch.

Agent ad litem: Song Guiping, Attorney at Xinjiang Foreign Economic and Trade Law Firm.

Defendant: Xinjiang Xinxing Water Resources and Electric Power Industry General Corporation.

Legal Representative: Gao Xingzhi, General Manager.

Agent ad litem: Ke Changjian, Deputy General Manager, Xinjiang Xinxing Water Resources and Electric Power Industry General Corporation.

Agent ad litem: Dong Yi, Deputy Director, Urumqi Sanyuan Law Office.

The plaintiff, Bank of China Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region Branch (hereinafter referred to as "Xinjiang Branch"), brought an action before the High People's Court of Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region against the defendant, Xinjiang Xinxing Water Resources and Electric Power Industry General Corporation (hereinafter referred to as "Xinxing Company"), concerning a dispute over a letter of credit transaction.

The plaintiff alleged: The defendant, as the beneficiary of a letter of credit transaction, applied for outward documentary bills while requesting negotiation from our bank. Our bank accepted the application and provided the defendant with export outward documentary bills in the amount of USD 840,000. After the letter of credit transaction was dishonored by the confirming bank due to discrepancies in the documents, the defendant refused to repay the funds advanced by our bank in accordance with its written undertaking. We request an order that the defendant repay the principal and interest of the advanced funds, as well as other economic losses, totaling RMB 10,031,627.78.

The defendant argued: The dishonor of this letter of credit transaction by the confirming bank was due to the plaintiff's failure to examine the documents with reasonable care in accordance with the provisions of International Chamber of Commerce Publication No. 500, Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credits (hereinafter referred to as UCP500), resulting in discrepancies. The plaintiff should bear responsibility for this. The undertaking made by our company to repay the outward documentary bills was conditional on the occurrence of "unexpected circumstances not within the scope of banking operations." Examining documents with reasonable care is a duty within the scope of banking operations. The plaintiff took the text out of context and misinterpreted our company's undertaking. Furthermore, the plaintiff's claim for repayment is based on the right of recourse of a holder in due course in a negotiable instrument relationship. The plaintiff failed to present to our company, within the prescribed time limit, the proof of dishonor by the foreign bank and has therefore lost its right of recourse against prior parties. The court should dismiss the plaintiff's claims.

The High People's Court of Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region found through trial: In October 1995, the defendant, Xinxing Company, entered into an import and export contract with Ukrainian Nelia Company for 120 tons of onion seeds. Subsequently, on October 17 of the same month, the plaintiff, Xinjiang Branch, received an irrevocable standby letter of credit issued by Ukrainian Slavic Commercial Bank and confirmed by Frankfurt Bank of Germany, with number 99519I1610, applicant being Ukrainian Nelia Company, beneficiary being Xinxing Company, and amount being USD 840,000. After verifying the signature and test key of the letter of credit, Xinjiang Branch notified Xinxing Company. Xinxing Company, claiming it was using the letter of credit settlement method for the first time and was unfamiliar with the operational procedures, orally instructed Xinjiang Branch to provide specific guidance and prepare relevant documents on its behalf, but never proposed any amendments to the terms of the letter of credit. Thereafter, Xinxing Company prepared the export goods as required by the letter of credit and submitted the relevant documents under the letter of credit to Xinjiang Branch on November 22, requesting negotiation. During the document examination, Xinjiang Branch noticed that the column for transport document requirements in the letter of credit stated "CMR (Convention on the Contract for the International Carriage of Goods by Road) transport document" in parentheses. It telephoned the carrier to inquire and, upon receiving an affirmative answer that it was a CMR transport document, concluded the document examination. While sending the documents to the foreign confirming bank for confirmation, Xinjiang Branch accepted Xinxing Company's application, took Xinxing Company's documents as collateral, and provided it with outward documentary bills of RMB 6,965,952 (equivalent to USD 840,000) for a term of three months. The next day, Xinxing Company submitted to Xinjiang Branch a written undertaking stating: "The sum of USD 840,000 is in fact funds advanced by Xinjiang Branch. If, during the settlement with Frankfurt Bank under the letter of credit by Xinjiang Branch, there arises any unexpected circumstance not within the scope of your bank's business operations, our company undertakes to repay the said funds." The documents sent by Xinjiang Branch to the confirming bank for confirmation were dishonored by the confirming bank on the ground that the transport document did not comply with the requirements of the letter of credit.

It was further found that the outward documentary bills were originally due on February 22, 1996. While notifying the defendant, Xinxing Company, of the maturity of the bills, the plaintiff, Xinjiang Branch, also extended the maturity on two occasions to December 20 of the same year. As Xinxing Company failed to repay, Xinjiang Branch filed the lawsuit on December 24, 1996. The High People's Court of Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region held: This case is a dispute arising from the use of letters of credit in international trade. In accordance with Article 142 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the PRC and pursuant to the agreement of the parties in the letter of credit, the provisions of UCP500 may be applied to determine the responsibilities of the parties in the letter of credit settlement.

I. Article 7(a) of UCP500 provides: "A credit may be advised to a Beneficiary through another bank (the Advising Bank) without engagement on the part of the Advising Bank, but that bank, if it elects to advise the credit, shall take reasonable care to check the apparent authenticity of the credit which it advises." The plaintiff, Xinjiang Branch, while acting as the advising bank, received the letter of credit from the foreign bank, verified the signature and test key, and then advised the beneficiary, thereby ensuring the apparent authenticity of the letter of credit and fulfilling its duty of reasonable care as an advising bank. During the stage of examining the letter of credit, Xinjiang Branch was not required to bear any liability.

II. According to the settlement procedures for letters of credit under UCP500, after receiving the letter of credit advised or transmitted by the advising bank, the beneficiary should carefully examine the letter of credit against the international sales contract to check for any terms that the beneficiary does not agree with or cannot accept. If any such terms exist, the beneficiary should promptly notify the applicant (buyer) to amend the letter of credit. China has not acceded to the Convention on the Contract for the International Carriage of Goods by Road (CMR) mentioned in the letter of credit, so Chinese carriers cannot issue "CMR" transport documents. Since the defendant, Xinxing Company, intended to use a domestic company for carriage, this term of the letter of credit could not be fulfilled. This was the root cause of the subsequent dishonor by the confirming bank on the ground of documentary discrepancies. After receiving the advice, Xinxing Company never proposed any amendment or objection to this term of the letter of credit, leading to the documentary discrepancy. Xinxing Company was at fault and should bear primary responsibility.

Article 3(a) of UCP500 provides: "Credits, by their nature, are separate transactions from the sales or other contract(s) on which they may be based and banks are in no way concerned with or bound by such contract(s), even if any reference whatsoever to such contract(s) is included in the credit." Although the defendant, Xinxing Company, had an oral agreement with the plaintiff, Xinjiang Branch, entrusting the latter to provide specific guidance and prepare relevant documents, the duty of Xinjiang Branch as the advising bank was only to verify the authenticity of the letter of credit. It had no obligation to examine the underlying contract or to assist the beneficiary in amending or performing the terms of the letter of credit. Xinxing Company's argument that the dishonor was due to Xinjiang Branch's failure to fulfill its duties within the scope of banking operations is untenable.

III. After the beneficiary of a letter of credit applies for negotiation, the bank that accepts the application begins the work of examining the documents. Article 13(a) of UCP500 provides: "Banks must examine all documents stipulated in the Credit with reasonable care, to ascertain whether or not they appear, on their face, to be in compliance with the terms and conditions of the Credit." The plaintiff, Xinjiang Branch, accepted the entrustment to provide specific guidance for this international export trade business. When examining the documents submitted by Xinxing Company, it noticed that the letter of credit required a "CMR" transport document. However, it only telephoned the carrier to inquire, without verifying with a person having specialized knowledge. It lightly believed that the documents were in compliance and sent them to the confirming bank for confirmation, resulting in dishonor. During the stage of examining the documents, Xinjiang Branch failed to exercise reasonable care in document examination and was negligent. It should bear corresponding liability.

IV. Article 10(b)(ii) of UCP500 provides: "Negotiation means the giving of value for Draft(s) and/or document(s) by the bank authorized to negotiate. Mere examination of the documents without giving value does not constitute a negotiation." After receiving the defendant Xinxing Company's application for negotiation and the attached documents, the plaintiff, Xinjiang Branch, paid Xinxing Company RMB 6,965,952 after examining the documents. However, this was not the giving of value for the documents by the bank, but rather the provision of outward documentary bills to Xinxing Company using the documents as collateral. This act does not constitute negotiation under UCP500. The interpretation of outward documentary bills in the Bank of China's "Basic Provisions on International Settlement Operations" is: Outward documentary bills are a form of financing in which a bank, using the complete and correct shipping documents provided by the exporter under a letter of credit as collateral, provides funds to the exporter with recourse reserved, before receiving payment from the issuing bank. In the written undertaking given to Xinjiang Branch after receiving the outward documentary bills, Xinxing Company also acknowledged that this outward documentary bills were funds advanced by Xinjiang Branch. Therefore, the ownership of these outward documentary bills belongs to Xinjiang Branch, while the ownership of the pledged documents still belongs to Xinxing Company. The relationship between the parties is a civil law obligation relationship, not a negotiable instrument relationship, and should be governed by Article 108 of the General Principles of the Civil Law.

V. Due to its own fault, the defendant, Xinxing Company, was unable to perform its obligations in the export trade as required by the terms of the letter of credit, and consequently could not obtain the consideration for the export trade through the letter of credit settlement. According to Article 108 of the General Principles of the Civil Law, Xinxing Company should bear the civil liability to return the funds advanced by the plaintiff, Xinjiang Branch, and to compensate for the interest loss on these funds during the period of use.

The plaintiff, Xinjiang Branch, failed to examine the documents with reasonable care and should bear the interest loss on the advanced funds after the dishonor. It is estimated that this portion of the loss accounts for 20% of the total interest loss during the period the funds were advanced by Xinjiang Branch. Xinjiang Branch should bear its own travel expenses incurred during the period of negotiations with the foreign bank after the dishonor.

Accordingly, on July 28, 1997, the High People's Court of Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region rendered the following judgment:

1. Xinxing Company shall repay to Xinjiang Branch the advanced funds of RMB 6,965,952.

2. The interest loss on the funds advanced by Xinjiang Branch, totaling RMB 1,332,238, shall be borne by Xinxing Company in the amount of 80%, i.e., RMB 1,065,790.40, and by Xinjiang Branch in the amount of 20%, i.e., RMB 266,447.60.

The total of the above two items, payable by Xinxing Company to Xinjiang Branch, is RMB 8,031,742.40. This shall be fulfilled within 10 days from the effective date of the judgment. For any delay in performance, interest on the debt for the delayed period shall be doubled.

Court acceptance fee: RMB 60,168.17; preservation fee: RMB 30,520; total: RMB 90,688.17. Xinjiang Branch shall bear 20%, i.e., RMB 18,137.63; Xinxing Company shall bear 80%, i.e., RMB 72,550.54.

After the first-instance judgment was pronounced, neither party filed an appeal within the statutory time limit.
